title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 4
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: The Evolution of Written Language
passages.text:
Writing systems represent one of humanity's most transformative inventions, fundamentally reshaping how societies preserve knowledge, conduct trade, and transmit culture across generations. The evolution of written language was neither a sudden breakthrough nor the work of a single culture; rather, it emerged gradually through the adaptation of existing symbols and communication systems in response to specific social and economic pressures.

The earliest written systems arose independently in several world regions around similar time periods, suggesting that writing fulfills a universal human need once societies reach a certain level of organizational complexity. The Sumerians of ancient Mesopotamia developed cuneiform around 3200 BCE, initially as a system for recording agricultural transactions and inventories. Similarly, Egyptian hieroglyphics emerged roughly contemporaneously, serving administrative and religious purposes. Chinese characters appeared approximately 1200 BCE during the Shang Dynasty, originally inscribed on oracle bones for divination. These systems share a crucial feature: they all began as logographic or pictographic in nature — representing whole words or meaningful concepts through visual symbols — before gradually incorporating phonetic elements that represented sounds rather than meanings.

The transition from logographic to alphabetic writing marked a revolutionary step in linguistic efficiency. While logographic systems require learning thousands of distinct characters to achieve literacy, alphabetic systems reduce writing to a manageable set of phonetic symbols representing sounds. The Phoenicians, a maritime trading culture around 1000 BCE, developed one of the first true alphabetic systems, which subsequent Greek, Hebrew, and Latin alphabets derived from. This shift democratized literacy: societies no longer needed to maintain a specialized scribe class requiring decades of training to master complex character sets. Ordinary merchants, soldiers, and craftspeople could relatively quickly learn to read and write, exponentially increasing the proportion of the population that could access written information.

Subsequent technological developments amplified writing's social impact. Paper technology, invented in China around the 2nd century CE, provided a more affordable and portable writing surface than papyrus or parchment, accelerating the spread of written texts. The printing press, perfected by Johannes Gutenberg in the 15th century, transformed writing from a labor-intensive manual craft into a reproducible commodity, catalyzing the Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment by making knowledge available to broader populations. Each innovation in writing technology—from paper to printing to digital text — has restructured how information flows through society.

Today, written language exists in unprecedented multiplicity. Alongside traditional orthographic systems, digital platforms have spawned new hybrid forms: acronyms, emojis, and abbreviated notation reshape linguistic conventions in real time. Yet the fundamental principle underlying all these variants remains unchanged: writing externalizes human thought, converting ephemeral speech into persistent symbols that transcend the limitations of human memory and geography.

passages.title: Plate Tectonics and Continental Drift
passages.text:
For much of geological history, scientists puzzled over striking similarities in fossil records and rock formations across continents separated by vast oceans. In the early 20th century, Alfred Wegener proposed a bold hypothesis: the continents themselves had not remained static but had slowly drifted across Earth's surface. Though initially ridiculed by the scientific establishment, Wegener's continental drift theory eventually became the foundation for the modern theory of plate tectonics, which now stands as the central organizing principle of Earth science.

Wegener's observations were compelling but initially lacked a mechanistic explanation for how continents could move. Fossils of identical species appeared on Africa and South America, separated by 3,000 kilometers of ocean. Mountain ranges and rock formations showed remarkable continuity across continental margins, suggesting these landmasses were once contiguous. Most tellingly, the coastlines of continents like South America and Africa appeared to fit together like puzzle pieces. Wegener proposed that all continents had once formed a supercontinent he named Pangaea, which subsequently fragmented and dispersed. However, without an explanation for the driving force behind this movement, his theory remained speculative until mid-century technological advances provided crucial evidence.

The discovery of seafloor spreading in the 1960s revolutionized understanding of plate tectonics. Scientists observing the Mid-Ocean Ridges — underwater mountain chains running through ocean basins — found that new oceanic crust constantly forms at these ridges through the upwelling of hot mantle material. As magma erupts and cools at ridge axes, it creates new seafloor that pushes older oceanic crust outward in both directions. This mechanism finally explained the driving force behind continental motion: the plates are carried passively on the conveyor belt of newly-formed seafloor. Magnetic striping patterns in oceanic rocks, which record reversals in Earth's magnetic field, provided the chronological framework demonstrating that seafloor spreading had occurred at measurable, consistent rates over millions of years.

Plate tectonics unifies disparate geological phenomena. Earthquakes concentrate along plate boundaries where friction between colliding or sliding plates releases accumulated stress. Volcanic activity clusters where subduction — the sinking of oceanic crust beneath lighter continental crust — triggers partial melting of the mantle. Mountain ranges rise where continental plates collide, buckle, and deform under immense compressional force. Understanding these processes through plate tectonics has transformed earthquake and volcano prediction, allowing societies to better prepare for geological hazards and mitigate risks to population centers.

The implications extend beyond geology to climate science and biology. The positions of continents influence ocean circulation patterns and atmospheric circulation, which regulate global climate. The distribution of species reflects both current geography and past continental positions, as organisms encountered novel selective pressures when continental reorganization altered habitats. Plate tectonics thus provides a unified framework for interpreting Earth's 4.5-billion-year history, demonstrating how the planet's surface is in constant, dynamic flux.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT true about the earliest written systems?
questions.correctAnswer: They all originated in Egypt
questions.explanation: The passage states that writing arose independently in several world regions (Mesopotamia, Egypt, China), not that they all originated in Egypt.
options: They served both administrative and religious purposes
They all originated in Egypt
They began as pictographic or logographic
They emerged in response to organizational complexity

questions.prompt: The word 'ephemeral' in the final paragraph is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: temporary and fleeting
questions.explanation: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time or temporary; the passage contrasts it with 'persistent symbols.'
options: complicated and technical
temporary and fleeting
repeated and frequent
audible and clear

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what major advantage did alphabetic systems provide over logographic systems?
questions.correctAnswer: They required learning far fewer symbols
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states alphabetic systems 'reduce writing to a manageable set of phonetic symbols' while logographic systems 'require learning thousands of distinct characters.'
options: They were invented earlier in human history
They required learning far fewer symbols
They could represent abstract concepts better
They were easier to paint on cave walls

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from the passage about the relationship between literacy rates and the development of alphabetic writing?
questions.correctAnswer: Alphabetic systems made widespread literacy more feasible
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains that alphabetic writing 'democratized literacy' and allowed ordinary people to learn quickly, implying higher potential literacy rates.
options: Alphabetic writing caused literacy rates to decline
Alphabetic systems made widespread literacy more feasible
Literacy rates were always equally high regardless of writing system
Only scribes benefited from alphabetic systems

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention the printing press in paragraph 4?
questions.correctAnswer: To illustrate how technological innovations amplified writing's social impact
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 discusses printing as one example among several technologies that transformed the reach and accessibility of written information.
options: To argue that paper was invented before the printing press
To illustrate how technological innovations amplified writing's social impact
To suggest that digital writing is inferior to print
To prove that Gutenberg invented writing

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a technological development that affected writing?
questions.correctAnswer: The invention of the telephone
questions.explanation: The passage mentions paper, printing press, and digital text, but does not mention the telephone.
options: Paper technology
The printing press
The invention of the telephone
Digital text platforms

questions.prompt: According to the passage, when did the Phoenicians develop an early alphabetic writing system?
questions.correctAnswer: Around 1000 BCE
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states the Phoenicians 'around 1000 BCE developed one of the first true alphabetic systems.'
options: Around 3200 BCE
Around 2000 BCE
Around 1000 BCE
Around 500 BCE

questions.prompt: The word 'catalyzing' in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: triggering or causing
questions.explanation: Catalyzing means bringing about or causing a process to happen; the printing press 'catalyzed' the Scientific Revolution.
options: delaying or preventing
triggering or causing
describing or analyzing
criticizing or opposing

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential meaning of: 'The Phoenicians, a maritime trading culture around 1000 BCE, developed one of the first true alphabetic systems, which subsequent Greek, Hebrew, and Latin alphabets derived from.'
questions.correctAnswer: The Phoenicians created an early alphabet that later alphabets were based on
questions.explanation: The sentence describes the Phoenicians' alphabetic contribution and its influence on later writing systems.
options: Greek and Latin alphabets existed before the Phoenician system
The Phoenicians created an early alphabet that later alphabets were based on
Maritime trade was the primary reason alphabets were invented
Hebrew is the oldest alphabet in the world

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.correctAnswer: A,C,E
questions.explanation: These three options capture the main ideas: writing's gradual independent emergence (A), the shift to alphabetic systems enabling broader literacy (C), and the impact of technological innovations (E).
options: A. Writing systems emerged independently in multiple regions as societies developed in complexity.
B. Cuneiform was the most important writing system ever developed.
C. The transition from logographic to alphabetic writing made literacy more accessible to ordinary people.
D. Emojis are more effective than traditional writing systems.
E. Technological innovations like paper and printing expanded the reach and accessibility of written information.
F. All ancient writing systems were completely phonetic from their origins.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what prevented Wegener's continental drift theory from being widely accepted initially?
questions.correctAnswer: It lacked a mechanism explaining how continents could move
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states Wegener's observations were 'compelling but initially lacked a mechanistic explanation for how continents could move.'
options: There was no fossil evidence supporting it
The continents had not actually moved
It lacked a mechanism explaining how continents could move
Alfred Wegener was not a credible scientist

questions.prompt: The word 'subduction' in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: the sinking of oceanic crust downward
questions.explanation: Subduction is explicitly defined in the passage as 'the sinking of oceanic crust beneath lighter continental crust.'
options: the spreading of new seafloor
the sinking of oceanic crust downward
the collision of tectonic plates
the formation of mountain ranges

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what evidence provided the chronological framework for seafloor spreading?
questions.correctAnswer: Magnetic striping patterns in oceanic rocks
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states 'Magnetic striping patterns in oceanic rocks, which record reversals in Earth's magnetic field, provided the chronological framework.'
options: Fossil records from continental margins
The fit between continental coastlines
Magnetic striping patterns in oceanic rocks
Measurements of ocean depth

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from the passage about the relationship between plate tectonics and volcanic activity?
questions.correctAnswer: Volcanic activity is concentrated where plates subduct
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains that volcanic activity 'clusters where subduction...triggers partial melting of the mantle,' establishing a direct causal relationship.
options: Volcanic activity occurs randomly across Earth's surface
Plate tectonics has no effect on volcanism
Volcanic activity is concentrated where plates subduct
Volcanoes only form at mountain ranges

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention the Mid-Ocean Ridges in paragraph 3?
questions.correctAnswer: To explain the physical mechanism driving continental movement
questions.explanation: The Mid-Ocean Ridges are presented as the location where seafloor spreading occurs, providing the mechanism that explained Wegener's observations.
options: To show that oceanic crust is older than continental crust
To explain the physical mechanism driving continental movement
To argue that Wegener's theory was entirely wrong
To describe the deepest parts of the ocean

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as evidence supporting continental drift?
questions.correctAnswer: The uniform temperature of all oceanic rocks
questions.explanation: The passage mentions fossil records, rock formations, coastline fit, and magnetic striping, but not uniform rock temperature.
options: Identical fossil species on different continents
Rock formations showing continuity across continental margins
Coastlines that fit together like puzzle pieces
The uniform temperature of all oceanic rocks

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does plate tectonics help explain the distribution of species?
questions.correctAnswer: Organisms adapted to new environments created by changing continental positions
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 states organisms 'encountered novel selective pressures when continental reorganization altered habitats,' linking species distribution to continental movement.
options: Species never change regardless of geography
Evolution occurs only on continental plates
Organisms adapted to new environments created by changing continental positions
All species originated from one continent

questions.prompt: The word 'contiguous' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: sharing a common border or touching
questions.explanation: Contiguous means sharing a common boundary or adjacent; the passage uses it to describe continents that were once joined together.
options: distant and separated
sharing a common border or touching
similar in composition
submerged under water

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential meaning of: 'Earthquakes concentrate along plate boundaries where friction between colliding or sliding plates releases accumulated stress.'
questions.correctAnswer: Earthquakes occur where tectonic plates meet and create friction
questions.explanation: The sentence explains the cause-and-effect relationship between plate boundaries and earthquake occurrence.
options: Earthquakes happen randomly everywhere on Earth
Plate boundaries prevent earthquakes from occurring
Earthquakes occur where tectonic plates meet and create friction
Stress accumulates only in the ocean

questions.prompt: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas in the passage.
questions.correctAnswer: A,B,D
questions.explanation: These capture the main themes: Wegener's initial observations (A), the discovery of seafloor spreading as the mechanism (B), and plate tectonics as a unifying framework (D).
options: A. Wegener observed striking similarities in fossils and rock formations across continents separated by oceans.
B. The discovery of seafloor spreading at Mid-Ocean Ridges finally explained how continents could move.
C. All continents are currently moving toward each other.
D. Plate tectonics explains earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain formation, climate, and species distribution.
E. Continental drift occurs only in the Atlantic Ocean.
F. Magnetic reversals on land are stronger than those in oceanic rocks.
